title: 9 49ers, 4 starters out injured in 2nd-to-last preseason practice
description: The San Francisco 49ers were missing 9 players, including two stars when they took the field for their second-to-last practice of the preseason.
fullText:
The San Francisco 49ers on Tuesday held their penultimate practice before boarding a plane for their flight to Australia where preparations for their Week 1 matchup against the Los Angeles Rams will begin in earnest. That practice came with some not-so-good news on the injury front.

According to ESPN's Nick Wagoner, nine players were not in attendance for the early part of Tuesday's session which is open to reporters. There were four projected starters among the group not participating. Here's the full list via Wagoner:

The silver lining here is that tight end George Kittle continued participating in practice which means he hasn't dealt with any setbacks. All signs continue to point toward him suiting up for the season opener.

It's important to note that Tuesday's practice isn't the indicator for which players will or won't be on the flight to Australia. The team is still likely exercising extreme caution with the regular season opener just over a week away. Getting to this point in the preseason and then pushing an injured player back into the fold too quickly would be a disaster.

On the other hand, it isn't a great sign that the 49ers still have so many key players listed as full absences. Wednesday will be a better indicator for who will and won't be making the trip. The 49ers aren't required to issue participation reports until Monday when their first regular practice week of the season begins.

title: HybridInfer: Local-first LLM router that falls back to cloud on failure
description: Reliability-aware local-first LLM router (pip): local model + automatic remote fallback when local stalls or crashes. - SimranKoul2026/HybridInfer-Python-tool
fullText:
Run LLMs on your own machine, without the crashes. HybridInfer is a
reliability-aware router: it sends each request to your local model first,
watches the local runtime in real time, and the moment local inference stalls,
crashes, or is predicted to fail, it transparently falls back to a remote
model. You keep local-first speed and privacy; you never get left with a wedged
model and no answer.

It runs as a local OpenAI-compatible server, so any tool that can talk to
the OpenAI API can point at HybridInfer and get smart routing for free.

The routing and reliability core is a Python port of the failure-aware
runtime-health controller from the HybridInfer research system
(https://github.com/SimranKoul2026/HybridInfer).

Running a model locally is cheap and private, but local runtimes wedge: long
prompts stall in prefill, the GPU runs out of memory, a driver hangs. Naive
"local only" setups then just hang. HybridInfer treats reliability as a
first-class routing signal:

You also need Ollama for the local tier:

Point any OpenAI client at it - streaming works too:

Or from the CLI: hybridinfer run --stream "...".

Every response carries a non-standard hybridinfer block telling you which tier
served it, whether it fell back, and the latency - safe for clients to ignore.
In streaming mode this metadata rides on the final chunk (the one with
finish_reason: "stop"), just before data: [DONE].

Streaming complicates fallback - once a token is on the wire it cannot be
un-sent. HybridInfer handles this with first-token-commit semantics:

title: GoPro Says It's Moving into Data Centers as Part of a $285M Merger
description: The company says its also planning a push into defense, robotics and aerospace.
fullText:
It's also planning a push into defense, robotics and aerospace.

GoPro is the latest surprising name to move into the AI data center market amid a merger with an optical-photonics company called Starman Optical. The shareholders of GoPro, which will remain publicly listed, will receive $285 million when the deal closes and retain around 10 percent ownership. GoPro's outstanding debt of around $92 million will be paid too.

The merger is subject to shareholder agreement, as well as regulatory approvals and closing conditions. GoPro expects the deal to close by the end of 2026.

Along with continuing to make its synonymous action cameras and run its subscription and cloud services, GoPro plans to move into new markets. Starman's optical transceivers are expected to fall under its umbrella, "extending the Company's reach into the large and rapidly growing market for AI infrastructure in optical transceivers," according to a press release. GoPro is also planning a push into the defense, government, robotics and aerospace sectors, bolstered by the combined company's IP, optics and imaging capabilities.

GoPro is following in the footsteps of shoemaker Allbirds by making an unexpected shift into AI infrastructure. As Reuters notes, GoPro briefly reached a valuation of $4 billion on its first day as a publicly traded company in 2014. Its stock has struggled in recent years, but the share price received a boost on Monday when it was revealed that YouTuber and filmmaker Markiplier (Mark Fischbach) had become GoPro's largest individual shareholder after acquiring an 8.5 percent stake.

title: Israel captures top Hamas commander in Gaza strike, defense minister says
description: Israel Katz says IDF forces captured Hamas security chief Mu'in al-Arabid during a deep raid in Gaza, with airstrikes covering the withdrawal.
fullText:
The Israel Defense Forces captured Hamas' head of general security during a raid in Gaza, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said.

An Israeli security official identified the Hamas leader as Mu'in al-Arabid, head of the General Security Apparatus, saying he was arrested during an Israeli incursion deep inside Hamas territory in Gaza. The IDF carried out airstrikes to cover the raid's withdrawal, adding that there were no Israeli casualties.

"A short time ago, a senior Hamas terrorist was arrested, and this is our policy: We do not wait for threats. Instead, we pursue Hamas terrorists, thwart them, and destroy their terrorist infrastructure. We have built a strong and unprecedented security zone in Gaza to protect residents and IDF soldiers," Katz said in a statement.

Hamas Struggles To Fill Leadership Ranks As Israel Hunts Oct 7 Terrorists

"Nearly 70% of the Gaza Strip has been destroyed, with no residents, no tunnels, and no homes, and the IDF controls the territory. We are not leaving Gaza until the Strip is demilitarized, Hamas is disarmed, and all terrorist tunnels are destroyed. Even after that, the IDF will remain in Gaza along defensive lines and ensure the security of the western Negev communities. Any attempt to bypass the security zone through aerial launches will be met with a harsh response," he added.

The raid comes weeks after President Donald Trump's administration demanded that Hamas disarm and give up control of Gaza in August. Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, traveled to Israel last month and said the IDF may receive U.S. backing to "finish the job."

Netanyahu Rejects Board Of Peace's Gaza Plan: No 'Withdrawal Until Hamas Is Genuinely Disarmed'

"If they don't follow through now on their commitment, everyone will see that they're not genuine about peace, and then Israel will have a lot more support from the U.S. and others to go and finish the job in the appropriate way," Kushner also told Fox News' Trey Yingst of the terrorist group.

The warning from Trump's son-in-law followed a rare face-to-face meeting with Hamas in Egypt — only Kushner's second known meeting with the group.

Kushner Touts Unprecedented Iran Contacts As Tehran Denies Trump Backchannel

"They said all the right things, but obviously, it's very, very hard to trust, you know, a terrorist organization that committed these terrible atrocities," Kushner continued. "But we had a very cordial meeting, and they said all the right things, and so we're going to give them a chance to perform."

"It's going to have to be based on actions and steps, and I hope it will be true."

The U.S.-led "Board of Peace" proposal centers on a phased ceasefire, demilitarization of Gaza, Israeli troop withdrawal, Palestinian technocratic governance and international reconstruction efforts.

title: Obama-era mandate slashed after being blamed for 'skyrocketing' housing costs
description: A new Trump admin housing directive aims to tackle the U.S.'s housing affordability crunch by ending Obama-era rule allowing indefinite liability for property owners over past building design errors.
fullText:
FIRST ON FOX: In a bid to tackle the nation's housing affordability crisis, the Trump administration has scrapped a controversial Obama-era mandate blamed for driving up property costs and stifling the affordable housing supply.

The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), alongside the Department of Justice, jointly rescinded an Obama-era policy that allowed third parties to file accessibility-related complaints over original building design flaws indefinitely, putting subsequent building owners on the hook for millions of dollars years after a project is completed, even if they were not the original builders.

According to internal agency data, the previous policy forced property owners to spend more than $112 million in accessibility retrofits over the last five years just to qualify for Federal Housing Administration (FHA) refinancing—costs that HUD says directly choked off affordable housing supply.

The rule eliminates the ability to hold current property owners indefinitely liable for architectural deviations committed by original builders decades in the past. Under the updated enforcement framework, the clock for filing Fair Housing Act design and construction challenges begins on the exact date a building receives its official certificate of occupancy.

One Unexpected Price Surge Most Americans Don't See Is Raising The Stakes For Trump Before November

Individuals or advocacy groups now have a strict one-year deadline to file administrative complaints directly with HUD. For private civil lawsuits filed in federal court, the statute of limitations caps claims at two years from the completion of construction.

Once those respective windows close, property owners are shielded from retroactive, building-wide liability for original architectural flaws, though individual tenants retain the right to seek reasonable modifications for their specific housing needs at any time under existing Fair Housing Act protections.

"[The Obama-era regulation] dramatically expanded the scope of the Fair Housing Act by declaring that deviations from HUD's accessibility guidelines, at the point of initial construction, gave rise to strict liability against the builder in perpetuity," the new guidance says. "That interpretation was egregiously wrong. It exceeded the Department's statutory authority, failed to increase the supply of accessible housing for individuals with disabilities, and imposed an unwarranted and unduly prejudicial burden on American homebuilders."

According to internal transaction data and industry reports provided to HUD, the financial toll of the previous policy extended far beyond standard compliance fees typically associated with federally-backed refinancing. For example, a single third-party housing inspection firm identified nearly $49 million in required accessibility fixes across almost 500 refinance deals since 2019—averaging over $100,000 in deficiencies per property.

Industry insiders and lenders also report that the Obama-era rules severely choked off financing, with one major affordable multifamily lender attributing more than $1 billion in lost HUD-insured loan volume over the last four years to the guidance, according to internal HUD data. Lenders told the agency that the ongoing uncertainty triggered recurring deal dropouts and discouraged prospective borrowers from pursuing FHA financing altogether.

Newsom Targets Major Affordability Squeeze In 'Striking' Convergence With Trump

"For too long, unnecessary government policies have contributed to the skyrocketing cost of building, buying, and renting a home. Today's action rescinds unnecessary and expensive liability created by legal theories that have no basis in law," said HUD Secretary Scott Turner. "The Trump Administration is following the law as written by Congress and interpreted by the courts. We will continue to repeal and replace guidance that does not honor these lawful commitments while ensuring Americans can access affordable housing."

At the heart of the administration's rollback is a fundamental legal principle that federal agencies cannot rewrite laws passed by lawmakers, nor can they ignore rulings by federal judges. When Congress updated the Fair Housing Act in 1988, lawmakers built in a strict one-year deadline to file administrative complaints. HUD officials argue the 2013 Obama-era policy effectively ignored that congressional mandate by allowing property owners to be targeted decades after a project was completed.

The shift also aligns federal enforcement with appellate court rulings, including a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. Judges in that case ruled that the illegal act of failing to properly design a building ends when construction wraps up and an official certificate of occupancy is issued.

"Congress wrote a clear statute of limitations into the Fair Housing Act. That limitation is part of the law, not a suggestion for sly bureaucrats to disregard," said Assistant Secretary for Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity Craig Trainor. "We will not allow Obama-era guidance to rewrite the Fair Housing Act, expose American builders to indefinite legal liability, and make housing less affordable for hardworking American families."

title: As Gen Z flocks back to accounting, EY is investing $100 million in bonuses for employees who prove they have human skills
description: EY is betting on human skills like judgment and adaptability, offering workers cash awards of up to $25,000 as AI transforms accounting.
fullText:
AI has made accounting cool again, as productivity gains take some of the "boring" tasks off employees' plates and make the profession more attractive to Gen Z looking for stable, high-paying work. But the technology is also creating a new challenge for the industry: convincing clients that the human expertise behind the work is still worth paying for.

Why is EY investing $100 million in employee skills?

What human skills remain valuable in AI-driven accounting?

How is AI changing entry-level accounting career paths?

Why are new accounting hires quitting so quickly?

Ernst & Young is betting that it is. The Big Four professional-services giant is planning to spend $100 million to reward U.S. employees who develop "future-focused" human skills, such as business acumen, judgment and adaptability, and experiment with technology to drive innovation and improve client services.

Individuals can earn spot awards up to $500, while individuals and teams whose work makes a material difference to the firm can receive cash awards up to $25,000, according to the Wall Street Journal.

"How we reward our people defines what we value as a firm. And what we value are confident professionals who continuously push themselves to learn fast and drive a lasting impact," EY Americas Chief Talent and Culture Officer Ginnie Carlier said in a press release.

"With these awards, we are empowering our EY professionals to bring a curious mindset to their work, to challenge what is possible and to ultimately shape the future of EY US."

EY's move comes as firms are asking employees to become more fluent in AI without losing the distinct human skills that can't easily be automated. For younger workers entering the industry, that balancing act is already becoming a complicated, but central part of preparing for a career.

Young workers and employees alike are aware of the need to protect human skills.

At fellow accounting firm KPMG, 76% of its latest summer intern cohort said future career success will require both strong human skills and the ability to effectively direct AI. At the same time, 43% worried that overreliance on technology could limit their critical-thinking abilities—suggesting that young workers are already thinking carefully about which skills they need to protect as AI takes on more of their work.

"For early-career professionals who aspire to leadership roles, the ability to evaluate information, apply context, exercise sound judgment and explain the 'why' behind a recommendation will be critical," Derek Thomas, KPMG U.S.'s national partner-in-charge of university talent acquisition, previously told Fortune.

title: He killed his 16-year-old ex-girlfriend 50 years ago. Florida just executed him.
description: The state executed Harold Gene Lucas by lethal injection for the 1976 murder of 16-year-old Jill Piper. Lucas was 24 at the time of the crime and was on death row for 50 years.
fullText:
Florida has executed a 74-year-old inmate who spent five decades on death row for shooting his teenage ex-girlfriend seven times even as she begged for her life. It's the first of eight scheduled executions in the U.S. in September, the most in a single month since 2010.

The state executed Harold Gene Lucas by lethal injection on Tuesday, Sept. 1, for the 1976 murder of 16-year-old Jill Piper in Bonita Springs, halfway between Fort Myers and Naples on Florida's Gulf Coast. Lucas was 24 at the time of murder.

Lucas, who was pronounced dead at 6:18 p.m. ET, became the 14th inmate executed in Florida this year, by far the most of any state. Florida governor Ron DeSantis continues an aggressive death penalty push as the end of his term approaches.

Lucas chose to accept his execution and waive further appeals after DeSantis signed his death warrant in July.

"I am 75 years old," Lucas recently told a court, though his 75th birthday would have been on Halloween. "I've been on death row for 50 years, and I have no desire to carry this any further . . . The sooner it's over, the better I'll enjoy it. I am tired."

Jill's brother, Buck Piper, told the Gulf Coast News that his father died waiting for justice but said that his 86-year-old mother would be front and center among the witnesses to the execution.

"They never got over the loss of their daughter," he told the station. "It's something that still weighs on her mind to this day."

Here's what you need to know about the execution, the crime, and why September is setting up to be the busiest single month for executions in 16 years.

On Aug. 14, 1976, Lucas had been drinking and doing hard drugs, got in a fight at a gas station, and told his friends he was going to "put that little (expletive) in a hole," according to court documents.

As Jill was returning home from a dance around midnight with two friends − 17-year-old Terri Rice and 19-year-old Richard Byrd Jr. − Lucas was lying in wait. Lucas fired four gunshots into Piper's back, and Rice and Byrd ran inside to call for help, court records say.

Though bleeding from the gunshot wounds, Piper was able to run inside. But Lucas followed, took her back outside and shot her three more times, including once in the back of the head, after she pleaded for her life. He then shot Byrd in the stomach and Rice in the hip. Both of them survived.

Lucas and Jill had dated for about four years when she broke up with him after an argument.

Part of the reason it has taken Florida so long to execute Lucas is because his death sentenced was vacated several times over the years, largely over procedural errors. Lucas has been re-sentenced to death altogether four times over the decades.

"It was an execution, pure and simple," prosecutor John Dommerich argued to jurors just before Lucas was sentenced to death for a fourth time in 1987, according to an archived story in the Naples Daily News, part of the USA TODAY Network. "He executed her when she begged for her life."

Lucas' attorneys had argued that he deserved mercy, saying he would never have killed Jill if he hadn't been drunk and high on hard drugs that night, including PCP.

At 16, Jill Piper was just getting started in life and was known for being just as sweet as she could be spunky, her younger brother, David Piper Jr., told the Naples Daily News on the 30th anniversary of her murder in 2006.

"She was tough," David Piper said at the time. "It was a scrappy little town here for many, many years, and she could take most of the guys, no problem ... But you can't fight bullets."

Even at 13, David Piper said he knew that Lucas was bad news and warned his sister to stay away from him. But, he said, Jill saw the good in everybody.

"She cared about people to the extreme," he said. "That's why she didn't get to live a long, fruitful life. Sometimes when people care to the extreme, they leave themselves wide open for dangerous situations to occur."

He told the newspaper that he tried not to think too much about his sister and didn't keep photos of her around.

"The only thing that will help is when Gene Lucas is put to death," he said.

Eight executions are scheduled to be carried out in five states this month. The executions include that of Christa Pike, the first woman set to be put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

The last time at least eight executions were carried out in a single month in the U.S. was in 2010, according to a USA TODAY analysis of data tracked by the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center. That year, five states carried out nine executions in the month of May.

This month's spate of executions comes amid an overall uptick in the death penalty in the U.S. in the last two years. In 2025, 11 states executed 47 inmates, the most in any single year since 2009. So far this year, 24 inmates have been executed, with another 13 on the calendar through December, though more are expected to be added.

Experts attribute the increases to a friendlier death penalty climate under President Donald Trump and Florida's particularly aggressive execution push in the last two years.

Of the 71 executions carried out in the U.S. since 2025, Florida accounts for 32 of them. That's 45%, and that figure is increasing. Of this year's 24 executions, Florida has carried out 14. That's 58%.

Gov. Ron DeSantis, who decides which inmates are executed and when, has been drawing increasing criticism from death penalty opponents and observers who say the governor is being motivated by political ambition ahead of the 2028 presidential election and is "increasingly treating executions as routine instruments of political power," according to a recent statement from Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty.

DeSantis, whose second term as governor ends in January, has said he wants to give closure to families who have waited for justice sometimes longer than four decades.

Amanda Lee Myers is a senior crime reporter who covers cold case investigations and the death penalty for USA TODAY. Follow her on X at @amandaleeusat.

title: Army secretary frequently warned White House about Hegseth: Sources
description: Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned early last week.
fullText:
Army Secretary Dan Driscoll's resignation follows a strained relationship with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and repeated warnings to the White House, including Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, about what has been described as Hegseth's widespread and seemingly indiscriminate firing of senior military officers, according to sources familiar with the matter.

Driscoll also warned the White House about unprecedented efforts by Hegseth to block others from advancing into the military's highest ranks after they had been thoroughly vetted, the sources said.

Driscoll resigned Monday last week at one of the busiest moments for the service since the height of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, creating a potentially significant leadership void as the Army takes on a growing list of demands.

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigns amid tensions with Hegseth

Driscoll also spoke with President Donald Trump last week when he submitted his resignation, according to two sources familiar with the conversation. He told Trump that Hegseth's chaotic removal of some of the Army's most experienced leaders, often with little or no explanation, was hurting the force and shrinking the pool of officers available for future senior commands, one of the sources explained.

Trump appeared surprised by the extent of the problem, the source said.

More than two dozen senior U.S. military officers have been fired or sidelined by Hegseth without any public explanation.

"The President has complete trust in Secretary Hegseth, who is doing an incredible job leading the Pentagon," Anna Kelly, a White House spokesperson said in a statement, adding that results in recent military operations, including the war in Iran "speak for themselves."

Iran live updates: After launching strikes, US warns of escalation if Iran responds

In a statement, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said, "Secretary Hegseth communicates with the president daily and is grateful to serve a commander-in-chief who loves our military," and he added that Hegseth "takes great pride in keeping the White House informed."

Driscoll arrived at the Pentagon as an unconventional choice. He had no national security experience and was a little-known figure whose background was largely in venture capital and Republican politics.

He served in the Army from 2007 to 2010 as a cavalry officer with the 10th Mountain Division and deployed to Iraq in 2009. He left the service as a first lieutenant, a junior officer rank that would have given him limited exposure to the large-scale operational planning and institutional management required to run the Army.

Army secretary calls fired general 'transformational' after Hegseth ousted him

In 2020, he ran unsuccessfully for North Carolina's 11th Congressional District, finishing sixth in a crowded Republican primary. He later advised the Trump-Vance transition team and worked for the Republican National Committee.

But Driscoll quickly became one of the most popular figures in national security circles and earned bipartisan support on Capitol Hill. Some of that goodwill came simply from contrast with Hegseth, according to officials familiar with the dynamics.

Driscoll was widely seen as less combative and positioned himself as a driving force for modernizing the Army through updating its doctrine and integrating robots, drones and other emerging technologies into the force.

"This is a big hit to the Army," one senior defense official said about Driscoll's exit, speaking on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to the press.

The official believed Driscoll had served as a buffer between Hegseth and the Army, particularly by pushing back through the White House on Hegseth's purge of senior officers, even if those efforts ultimately did little to slow it.

Driscoll befriended Vice President JD Vance years earlier when they attended Yale Law School together. That relationship was widely viewed as a key reason Hegseth was unable for a while to push Driscoll out despite tensions between the two.

Driscoll's popularity also grew from his work with Democrats, including Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., on so-called right-to-repair reforms aimed at cutting through Pentagon rules and defense industry restrictions that can prevent troops from fixing their own equipment. In many cases, defense companies require their own personnel to make repairs or replace parts, an expensive process that can leave equipment sidelined for months or even years.

The Army secretary job has often been marked by turnover, with acting officials and tenures of roughly two years or less being common in the past two decades. John McHugh was a notable exception, serving from 2009 to 2015 under President Barack Obama and becoming one of the longest-serving Army secretaries in recent decades.

Parnell, the Pentagon spokesperson and an Army veteran, is widely viewed as a potential replacement for Driscoll and has advocated for the job behind the scenes, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with the matter.

However, Parnell would face a difficult confirmation fight. He dropped out of a Pennsylvania Senate race in November 2021 amid allegations from his estranged wife of abuse during a contentious child custody case. Parnell has denied the allegations.

Driscoll's departure is the latest high-profile departure of a senior defense official during Hegseth's tenure.

In April, then-Navy Secretary John Phelan was abruptly forced out without explanation, as was Gen. Randy George, the Army's top officer at the time, serving as Driscoll's most senior advisor.

Hegseth blocks promotion of several Navy officers to 1-star rank

On Tuesday, former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall expressed concerns in a New York Times op-ed that the military's senior officers have chosen to keep a low profile when it comes to some of the Trump administration's actions involving the U.S. military, singling out Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

"When they aren't ignoring how abnormal things have become, they turn to the other approach, claiming that they have no responsibility for the actions the armed forces have been ordered to take because those orders were 'policy' choices outside the scope of their duties," wrote Kendall. "This is a cop-out, and it is putting our democracy at risk."

When asked about Kendall's comments, Joe Holstead, a spokesman for Caine, said: "The Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff remains focused on his responsibilities as principal military advisor to the President, the Secretary of War, and the National Security Council, which include providing best military advice and a range of military options along with all associated risks, impacts, and secondary considerations."

title: Exclusive-US may require parents to prove citizenship to get passports for their children
description: The U.S.
fullText:
Sept 1 (Reuters) - The U.S. State Department has proposed requiring parents applying for passports for their children to provide proof of their own citizenship or immigration status as part of President Donald Trump's latest effort to limit ‌birthright citizenship.

The draft guidance, reviewed by Reuters, is the first detailed look at how the State Department could enforce Trump's August 6 ‌executive order targeting what it calls "birth tourism" and broadening historical exceptions to birthright citizenship.

The White House referred Reuters questions to the State Department. In a statement, State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott ​said that "President Trump has been unequivocal that this Administration will protect the meaning and value of American citizenship, full stop, and that includes making sure our passport adjudication process fully reflects that standard."

Limiting birthright citizenship has been one of the president's top priorities in his far-reaching crackdown on immigration. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled his previous attempt violated the country's Constitution.

Trump's initial executive order would have granted automatic U.S. citizenship at birth only to children with at least one ‌parent who was a U.S. citizen or a lawful ⁠permanent resident known as a green card holder.

In a 6-3 ruling, the Supreme Court found the order was unlawful, with a majority finding it violated the Citizenship Clause of the Constitution's 14th Amendment.

Trump's August 6 order was ⁠narrower, taking particular aim at "birth tourism," in which women travel to the United States to give birth so their children can obtain automatic citizenship. That order could still be blocked in court.

The new directive would withhold citizenship from children with a parent who works for a foreign government in the U.S., is engaged in fraud or ​a ​commercial transaction to obtain citizenship, or is classified as an "alien enemy."

"The Department will require ​parental information and evidence of parental citizenship or immigration status ‌as part of its determination whether the applicant is subject to EO 14418," the State Department draft guidance reads, citing the executive order number.

If implemented, the proposal would require all parents or legal guardians to provide proof of their citizenship, such as a valid U.S. passport or birth certificate, or evidence of their immigration status, such as an I-94 form or a legal permanent residency card, when submitting a passport application for their children. The information would be used by the government to determine if the child qualifies for citizenship under the new order, the State Department proposal says.

Currently, parents whose children ‌were born in the U.S. only need to prove their parentage and present photo identification ​during this process. They are also asked to check a box on the application form ​indicating if they are U.S. citizens but are not required to file ​supporting documentation.

Lawyers pursuing class-action lawsuits on behalf of babies who would be deprived of citizenship under Trump's initial order ‌have asked two different federal judges to prevent his latest ​order from taking effect.

One of those lawsuits ​is before U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman, who was appointed by Democratic President Joe Biden.

At a hearing on Friday in Greenbelt, Maryland, Boardman voiced skepticism about what she called Trump's unprecedented order and allowed the plaintiffs to revise their lawsuit so she could consider whether to ​block it.

Justice Department attorneys have argued that a ‌restraining order would be inappropriate and that the legal challenge was premature, as federal agencies had yet to issue public guidance on ​how the president's directive would be implemented.

title: 'The search was over': A family's four-day quest for a son lost in Nepal's floods
description: For four agonising days after floodwaters tore through Nepal's Rasuwa district, Ayush Khadka's family searched desperately for any sign that
fullText:
CHITWAN, Nepal, Sept 1 (Reuters) - For four agonising days after floodwaters tore through Nepal's Rasuwa district, Ayush Khadka's family searched desperately for any sign that the 21-year-old civil servant was still alive.

The Khadkas were among thousands of families clinging to hope amid ‌the chaos wrought by a glacial collapse that sent an unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud and debris crashing through valley towns and villages ‌in Nepal and across the border in China.

Ayush had spoken to relatives the night before the flood, and his social media account even appeared to show him as online the following morning, ​a small sign that gave the family hope he had survived.

As reports of widespread destruction emerged on August 26, family members immediately began what would turn out to be a futile search.

For two days his paternal uncle, Ganesh Khadka, waited near the Nepali Army's Maithali Barrack in Nuwakot, one of the main coordination points for rescue and recovery efforts near the flood-ravaged region.

Despite repeatedly sharing Ayush's name, workplace and last known location in Timure with officials, the family received few answers, Ganesh said.

In a desperate ‌attempt to learn more, relatives tried to reach Timure — ⁠the badly flood-hit town where Ayush had been stationed, hundreds of kilometres from the family home in Salyan district — but roads had been destroyed and all private helicopters had been requisitioned by the government for rescue operations.

Meanwhile, Ayush's maternal aunt, Laxmi Thapa, ⁠was searching for him about 200 km (124 miles) away in Chitwan, where bodies had been swept downstream by the flood and were being recovered.

Unknown to most family members at the time, authorities had already recovered a body believed to be Ayush's on the day of the disaster, which has killed at least 939 people and left about 4,000 ​missing.

On ​August 27, Laxmi visited a temporary holding centre where photographs of recovered bodies were being ​displayed on a television screen for identification by relatives. One image ‌immediately caught her attention. "I was about 70% sure it was him," she said.

She sent the photograph to other relatives, including Ganesh, for their opinions, but the family deliberately chose not to show it to Ayush's distressed mother, Muna Khadka.

The family scrutinised every visible detail: a mole on the left side of the chin appeared to match Ayush's, as did his beard. They also recognised a black religious protection thread, known as a 'buti,' that he regularly wore on his left arm but had slipped towards his wrist.

Still, they remained unsure, and for days the search for Ayush continued.

Information arrived in fragments, often through unofficial ‌channels. The distance between Salyan, Kathmandu, Nuwakot, Chitwan and the flood-ravaged border region complicated every ​effort to establish what had happened.

The uncertainty became even more painful as authorities prepared for the ​mass burial of unidentified bodies.

The Khadka family feared that victims from distant ​districts could be buried before relatives had enough time to reach Chitwan and identify them.

It was not until August 30, ‌four days after the flood, that Ayush's mother was finally informed ​by the family that her son was ​dead.

The next morning, immediate and extended family members left Salyan at around 1 a.m. and travelled through the night to Chitwan. They arrived at around 8 a.m., exhausted after hours on the road but determined to obtain final confirmation.

There, standing before the recovered body, they confirmed what many ​had already feared.

Hours later, about 35 relatives gathered on the ‌banks of the Narayani River to cremate a young man whose family had spent days searching for a different outcome.

"We were so ​happy when he was born, and equally happy when he passed the civil service examination at such a young age," Laxmi said. "And now, ​he has left us in tears."

(Writing by Aftab Ahmed; Editing by Saad Sayeed)

Former President Joe Biden's son, Hunter Biden, said Sunday that former Vice President Kamala Harris was getting bad political advice after he refused to explain why he thinks she wasn't a good politician.

Biden said, "I think that this administration, unlike you, I don't think that she should have ever been any daylight between, she can make daylight between herself and my dad, but not in terms of what they were able to accomplish over that four-year period. I think that there might be daylight as issues related to Gaza and as it relates to Israel that of course, she needs to be able to stake her own ground on that."

The Zeteo founder noted that Harris didn't really break from Biden on Gaza or Israel.

Biden insisted Harris' refusal to break with his father on the issue didn't have anything to do with his father.

"He didn't pressure her? No daylight, kid?" Hasan asked.

A post-2024 election book by reporters Jonathan Allen and Amie Parnes said Joe Biden had told Harris repeatedly that there could be "no daylight" between them and reported that he told her, "No daylight, kid," during a call ahead of her debate with Donald Trump.

Kamala Harris Leaves Biden Off List Of Top Three 'Most Effective' Presidents

The former president denied doing this during an interview on "The View."

"Nothing to do with loyalty to my dad, from my perspective. But here's the thing, is this, is that, you know what? She's a free agent now. I'm Hunter Biden," he said. "I get to think whatever the hell that I want to think about anybody."

Hasan pressed him again, questioning, "I'm asking why do you think she's not a very good politician?"

"That's between me and her," Hunter Biden told Hasan.

Hasan responded and said, "You can't just dangle that out."

Hunter Biden Reveals He's 'Definitely Not Running' For Office Despite Media Tour

"You know why I can? Because I ain't running for anything, Mehdi, I can say whatever the f--- I want," Biden shot back.

Hunter Biden said he did not agree with the perspective that Harris was loyal to his father throughout her campaign.

"I think that she was loyal to my father, and I don't think she was loyal to a fault, however. There are certain things she was not loyal on. I think right now her recent appearances that I've seen and what she's trying to distance herself from my dad, the things that she wrote in her book, that we're not loyal in any way. And, so, there is not like this 100%," he said.

Later in the interview, during a discussion about a possible 2028 ticket, Biden said he would love for Harris to be president of the United States.

"I would love for her to be president of the United States. I think she would make a great president of the United States. I just think that, right now, she's getting bad political advice. That's it," he said.

Harris' office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

"She was so careful about showing loyalty to Biden that she never established a strong identity of her own. When she was asked what she would have done differently, she struggled to give voters a clear answer.

"Voters cast their vote on leadership, confidence and authenticity. If the country is unhappy with the person in charge, you can't run as the change candidate while essentially saying, 'I wouldn't have changed much.'"

Those Democrats backed a key GOP procedural vote that needed to succeed for Republicans to later bring several bills to the floor.

The reason? It helped pave the way for a priority bill for Golden supporting lobstermen, according to two people familiar with the discussion. The bill already has White House support, and Golden and others hope it can become law this year.

But their vote also allowed Johnson to proceed with messaging votes that Democrats oppose, including a resolution to condemn socialism that Republicans hope to use against Democrats on the campaign trail.

The defection of those two Democrats quickly enraged members of their own party — including some party leaders, who were shocked by the two members' votes, several people told CNN.

Asked whether he's disappointed in those members, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters: "The two Democrats who voted for the rule did not give any member of House Democratic leadership a heads-up, and as a result, blindsided the entire caucus and created a significant breach of trust."

Jeffries said it's "under discussion" whether the two lawmakers will face repercussions.

Golden said in a statement, "I voted for the rule for one simple reason: It paved the way for a vote on my bill to protect Maine lobstermen from costly, burdensome new regulations that would put them out of business."

"My constituents don't care about the team sports of Congressional procedure," he added.

Across the caucus, Democrats argued the defection in their ranks prevented a massive and embarrassing defeat for Republicans that could have forced Johnson to send members home for the rest of September.

Typically, members of the minority party stick together to oppose these kind of procedural votes, which the majority party needs to bring bills to the floor.

Multiple conservatives were blocking their party leaders' plans for the floor this week in an attempt to protest a separate move to pass a stopgap funding bill that's detested by the far right.

Republicans like Rep. Chip Roy refused to support a Senate-passed funding bill that didn't allow House conservatives to insert their own priorities, like provisions against what they call "mass surveillance" or more money for President Donald Trump's immigration agenda.

title: 10 Apple Health Hacks Every iPhone User Should Know
description: You don't need an Apple Watch to get great health insights from Apple.
fullText:
Even if you’ve never opened the Apple Health app, if you have an iPhone, you’ve probably used apps that send information to its on-phone database. Apple Health is a powerful tool for controlling who gets access to your health data, logging data in different ways, and even taking at-home screening tests for certain health issues. If you have an Apple Watch, that’s great, but you don’t need one (or any wearable!) to take advantage of most of these 10 hacks to get more out of the Apple Health app.

Before we get into the other hacks, I’d like to discuss just how private your Apple Health data is (or isn’t). Apple provides its Health privacy policy here, and it says that your data lives on your own device and is encrypted when your phone is locked. There are some exceptions, though, which you can turn on or off. Here are the main things you may want to check on:

Individual apps can ask for permission to read data from Apple Health. (They also need your permission to write data to it.) You can control per-app permissions in Settings. Or, for a specific data point (like “walking and running distance”), go to that area of Apple Health and tap Data Sources and Access.

You can back up your health data via iCloud, which means it will live on Apple’s servers so you can access it from any of your devices. It is encrypted so Apple cannot read it. Manage this from your iCloud settings (in Settings, under your name).

You can share health data with your doctor or with people you know, like family members. To manage who has access, go to the Health app and tap the Sharing tab.

During workouts, some data from your workout may appear in a Live Activity widget on your lock screen. To hide this data while your phone is locked, go to the Settings app, tap Face ID & Passcode, and then under Allow Access When Locked, toggle Workout Health Data.

Your Medical ID may be available when your device is locked. (This is how bystanders and first responders can access your emergency contact or other information you’d like to remain available in emergencies.) To control access to this, go to the Health app, find Medical ID, and toggle Show When Locked.

The Health app includes a built-in medication tracker with a number of hidden features. Browse or search for Medications, and set up tracking by adding a medication, or anything else. You can type in the name, or use your camera to scan the bottle’s label. (This also works for over-the-counter meds and supplements, like if you want to be sure to take a vitamin every day.) I like that you can customize a pill-shaped icon to match a pill’s appearance.

Next, you can set up reminders. From this screen, you can tell the app when you plan to take your medication (if it’s one you take regularly, rather than as needed). The Health app will notify you at that time. To make the most of this feature, I recommend setting up follow-up reminders, which you’ll find on a different screen as well—more about that below.

After you set up your medications, scroll to the bottom of the medications screen and tap Pin to Summary. Now you just have to open the Health app and tap Medications to see a list of what you need to take today. You can also log via Siri, including batched logging like “Siri, log that I took my 10 a.m. meds” so you don’t have to list each one.

At the bottom of the Medications screen, you can tap Options and turn on Follow Up Reminders, which will give you an extra notification 30 minutes after the first one if you haven’t logged a dose. I use this feature all the time myself: I get the first reminder while I’m in the middle of doing something, eventually take the pill, then the follow-up reminds me to log it. If I got distracted along the way, I have a second chance to not miss a dose.

Another handy feature here is the Export PDF button at the bottom of the page, which will print out a list of all your current medications so you can bring it to your medical appointments or anywhere else you need to.

If you’re not familiar with the Health app, you might not think there’s much there—just a few things on the home screen. You can change that, but it takes a few steps. You see, rather than being a minimalist app, there’s so much available in Health that Apple figures it’s not worth giving you a big list to start off. Tap the magnifying glass icon in the lower right corner, and you’ll see a whole list of categories. You can search from this screen, or browse the categories.

Definitely take a minute to browse through these and see what features you might actually use. If you track what you eat in an Apple Health-connected app, you’ll be able to see all the individual components here: how much protein you’ve gotten today, for instance. Anything that a wearable can track is on here, including things you probably didn’t realize. I have a grade for my walking steadiness, for example.

Once you’ve figured out which of these hundreds of data points are actually useful, put the ones you care about on the main app screen (called Summary). Find a relevant card by searching or browsing, scroll to the bottom, and tap Pin to Summary. This way you can see exactly what you want when you open the app: say, your steps, protein intake, and the day’s medications. (Plus a few things you may want to add after you learn about them below...)

A lot of us are nervous about logging reproductive health data anywhere that may not be private. I’ve written that Euki may be the best standalone app for privacy, but you don’t need to use an app at all: Tracking directly in Apple Health means that your data is encrypted and lives on your phone, subject to the privacy features discussed above.

To use the built-in tracker, go to the magnifying glass and tap (or search for) Cycle Tracking. The cycle tracker on this screen (which you can pin to your summary) allows you to log menstrual bleeding, as well as “factors” like contraceptive use, pregnancy, and more.

Under the Options at the bottom of this screen, you can turn on period predictions, fertile window estimates, and more. I recommend enabling the Symptoms log if you’d like to keep track of things like cramps and nausea. You can also decide if you want Apple Health to use your temperature and heart rate data from a wearable for better cycle detection.

Another surprising use for manual logging in the Health app is under Mental Wellbeing. This is a really useful screen, since it collects things known to affect mental health, like your sleep, exercise minutes, time in daylight, and more. From here, you can also set up emotion and mood logging. The app explains that it considers emotions to be how you feel right now, and moods are how you’ve felt overall that day.

You can turn on reminders to log your moods. The default is to log twice per day: once around midday, and once at the end of the day. Scroll to the bottom of the Mental Wellbeing screen to set up logging.  Once you’ve set it up, it will appear as State of Mind; you may want to pin this to your summary. You can even view graphs of your state of mind over time, and see what other factors they associate with. A really useful view is to tap Show in Charts and then highlight Life Factors so you can see if your moods seem to track your exercise minutes or your hours of sleep.

The Health app also includes a built-in hearing test, but it requires AirPods Pro 3 (or AirPods Pro 2). To find the hearing test, look up Hearing in the Health app, then Get More From Health, and then Take Hearing Test. This will only be available if you have the right type of headphones connected. Follow the prompts to take the test. Apple has more information on this test here. If your results seem concerning, you can export a PDF of your results to discuss with a professional.

Accessing your medical records through patient portals can be annoying. Instead, you can import your digital medical records directly into the Health app, giving you quick access to your medical history as needed. Apple offers a list of the healthcare systems whose data it can access.

It’s worth looking over the privacy policies for this feature as well, but the good news is that the data follows an encrypted connection between your phone and the healthcare organization, without ever giving Apple (the company) access to it. I’d recommend turning off Improve Health Records, which sends an anonymized version of your data to Apple; health records are detailed information about your body—but feel free to leave it on if that’s your preference. You can back up your health data over iCloud, as discussed above.

As with menstrual cycle tracking, it can be useful to any health data directly in the app. You can actually do this with just about any data point: just view that type of data, and then tap the plus sign in the upper right corner. Think you took about 1,000 steps when you had your watch off? Just tap the plus on the Steps screen and add them.

A handy place to use this feature is for blood pressure tracking. Some wearables estimate your blood pressure, like Whoop and the Samsung Galaxy Watch. But you don’t need one of those to log your numbers: just take note of your blood pressure at the doctor’s office, or when you use a wrist cuff or one of those machines they sometimes have at pharmacies. Open Blood Pressure and tap the plus, then put in the new reading. You’ll be able to view your history of blood pressure readings, and even see charts of how it has changed over time.

Some medications affect your heart rate, most notably beta blockers and calcium channel blockers. If you’re taking one of those, your heart rate won’t match Apple’s general-purpose formulas for gauging your cardio fitness (a VO2max estimate) from your heart rate. You’ll appear to have a higher cardio fitness than you actually have.

To let Apple account for this, go to your profile picture, tap Health Details, tap Edit at the top of the page, and scroll down to Medications That Affect Heart Rate. You can select calcium channel blockers or beta blockers, or both; these are the only categories of medication that Apple can account for.

There’s a Medical ID feature that can be accessed from your lock screen even without unlocking your phone. It’s a great place to put your emergency contact information, but to make the most use of it, you need the people in your life to know how to access the information and what’s in there.

I first learned about the Medical ID when I was teaching a class. A student came up to tell me about a medical condition, and showed me how to access her Medical ID (it’s right at the bottom of the lock screen). Most importantly, she made sure I knew what information I’d be able to find there, so I knew when and whether to reach for it in an emergency.

I’d advise that you do the same if you want to be prepared. Besides allergies and contact information, the Medical ID field can include information on whether you’re pregnant, what medications you take, any medical conditions you’d like to disclose, and your height, weight, and blood type. There’s also an area at the bottom for notes, where you can add any information you feel is critical.

Also consider whether you want to turn on Share During Emergency Call, which allows this information to be shared with emergency services. You can also control whether or not your Medical ID appears on your lock screen using a separate toggle.

title: 'I've got that spark back'- McMenamin on Glens return
description: Conor McMenamin says his short-lived move to Coleraine "was not meant to be" after his shock deadline day return to Glentoran.
fullText:
Conor McMenamin says his short-lived move to Coleraine "was not meant to be" after his shock deadline day return to Glentoran.

The 31-year-old joined the Bannsiders in June on a long-term deal from St Mirren but has now made an unexpected return to the Glens for his second spell at the club.

McMenamin scored 39 goals in 80 appearances for the east Belfast side before he moved to the Buddies in 2023.

"Before I went to Coleraine, Glentoran wasn't an option and, as soon as I found out that they were this time around, I said to my agent to get it done quick," McMenamin told BBC Sport NI's Stephen Watson.

"I'm delighted and I want to play with that smile and that freedom that I did before I came here.

"It's been pretty challenging the last two months for me, and I probably didn't really enjoy any of the last two months. Now I've got that spark back, I'm happy to be here, and I can't wait to get going."

McMenamin joins Glens two months after Coleraine move

McMenamin did not start a game for Coleraine during his short spell at the club and made three substitute appearances for the side in the Irish Premiership.

Despite the move failing to live up to the hopes that surrounded it, McMenamin added that it was "nobody's fault".

"It didn't work out at Coleraine and that is nobody's fault and I have no bad things to say about Coleraine," he continued.

"From a family and personal perspective, it was not meant to be. I am glad to be back here and playing football.

"I couldn't commit to living up there. It was too far to travel, and I have family in Downpatrick, and it just wasn't working out, and my partner is from Scotland. These things happen in football."

The Northern Ireland international made the move from the Glens to St Mirren in 2023 and made 64 appearances during his time at the Buddies.

He was also part of the St Mirren side that beat Celtic in the 2025-26 League Cup final.

Now, that experience of winning silverware is something that McMenamin hopes to bring back with him to the Glens.

"When I was in Scotland, I got a taste for winning trophies, and it was an unbelievable experience as a player, and this club deserves to win trophies," he continued.

"We have to be able to try and bring the league back here. That's what a big club should do and a big club should be ambitious to win trophies and I hope I can help fulfil that ambition.

"I'm here for a long time and, you know, I'm here to play well and I'm here to win games for Glentoran and I am excited for that."

McMenamin is also hopeful that the return to familiar surrounding may revive his international ambitions.

He has won 14 Northern Ireland caps but has not featured in a green and white shirt since June 2024.

The winger added that he has already spoken to Northern Ireland manager Michael O'Neill about his return to his former club and has no intention of closing the door on his international career.

"I actually spoke to Michael [O'Neill] about the move.

"That is something as a player that I'll never close the door on. It's the best memories of my career.

"I now need to do well for Glentoran before any of that happens. So, I'll just look forward and do well for Glentoran and hopefully Michael will ring my phone again."

title: Balogun's Everton deal collapses after he walks away
description: Everton's pursuit of Folarin Balogun from Monaco collapses after Balogun decides against move.
fullText:
Everton's move for Folarin Balogun collapsed after the player decided against proceeding with a transfer.

The deal was renegotiated after Everton initially agreed a £40m deal with Monaco for Balogun, 25, because of an issue with his medical.

The United States striker is understood to have decided against going ahead with the move.

Everton had submitted a deal sheet before the window closed at 23:00 BST to try to get the Balogun deal over the line.

Balogun had emerged as a late target after Guinea-Bissau frontman Beto completed a permanent move to Serie A club Fiorentina.

The Toffees did also explore moves for Manchester United striker Joshua Zirkzee and Aston Villa frontman Tammy Abraham, but were unable to convince either to join.

Grealish spent the 2025-26 season on loan with Everton, making 20 appearances, before sustaining a season-ending foot injury in January.

The 30-year-old had been linked with other teams - including boyhood club Aston Villa - but has opted to reunite with David Moyes on Merseyside.

"I think I'm at my best at everything in life, not just football, when I feel loved. That's what the manager has given me, what my teammates have given me and especially what the fans have given me," Grealish said.

"Every time I see an Everton fan, it's just pure love and the way they've welcomed me since that first game against Leeds, I'll never forget that."

Grealish, who joined City from Villa for £100m in August 2021, scored twice and provided six assists in 20 appearances during his previous spell with Everton - winning the Premier League Player of the Month for August.

The England international returned from injury during Manchester City's Community Shield defeat against Arsenal on 16 August.

He also featured under Enzo Maresca in City's opening game of the 2026-27 Premier League season as they beat Bournemouth 2-1.

The 29-year-old former Arsenal player has won five caps for England and can operate as a full-back or in midfield.

description: Tottenham sign Chelsea winger Mykhailo Mudryk on loan until the end of the season and complete a permanent move for Tosin Adarabioyo.
fullText:
Tottenham have signed winger Mykhailo Mudryk and defender Tosin Adarabioyo from Chelsea on transfer deadline day.

Mudryk joins Spurs on loan until the end of the season while 28-year-old centre-back Adarabioyo has completed a permanent move worth up to £12m to the north London side.

As part of the agreement, Spurs have the option to turn Mudryk's move permanent for £75m.

The move reunites the Ukraine international, 25, with Spurs boss Roberto de Zerbi, who was his manager at Shakhtar Donetsk before his move to Chelsea in 2023.

"It's a great feeling and I can't wait to start training and playing for the club," Mudryk said.

"I'm a player who brings speed and creativity, and I want to help in both the offensive and defensive areas. I want to make the fans excited.

"I can see it's a strong squad here with good players, and I'm looking forward to sharing a pitch and special moments with them."

Mudryk resolved a doping case with the Football Association last month, but has not played a competitive match since November 2024.

Meanwhile, Adarabioyo's move makes him Spurs' 10th signing during a busy summer that has seen them spend over £300m on transfers.

"I'm in an important part of my career and speaking to the head coach and knowing the type of football he wants to play, I think it's a very good fit," Adarabioyo said.

"He wants the team to play with courage and that's something that I always look to do. I want to achieve the absolute best, to push this team and this club as much as possible to where we deserve to be."

The former England Under-19 international made 70 appearances for Chelsea since joining from Fulham in the summer of 2024.

He will replace Kevin Danso at Spurs following the Austria international's loan move to Sunderland.

Mudryk took part in Chelsea's pre-season tour of Australia and Asia, where he made his return in a friendly against Juventus in Hong Kong.

However, he was not included in Xabi Alonso's squad for the Premier League victories against Fulham and Brighton, or the Carabao Cup win against Luton.

Chelsea had been in talks with Leeds and rejected at least one offer for Mudryk, but Spurs entered the race at a late stage after failing in attempts to sign Iliman Ndiaye, who has since joined Manchester City from Everton, and Liverpool attacker Cody Gakpo.

"Having worked with Misha earlier in his career, I know exactly what he can bring to our team," said De Zerbi.

"He has the quality to change a game with his speed and ability in one-vs-one situations, and is an exciting, attacking talent.

"I will demand a lot from Misha and it is our job to help him find the best version of himself. If we do that then he can become a very important player for us. I am very happy he chose to come here, and I cannot wait to work with him again."

He scored 10 goals and provided 11 assists in 73 games in all competitions for Chelsea.

Mudryk joined Chelsea from Shakhtar in 2023 for an initial £61m, having attracted interest from clubs across Europe including Arsenal.

After impressing in the Champions League with Shakhtar in the first half of 2022-23, Mudryk needed time to adapt to a new country and league.

He had to wait until October 2023 for his first Chelsea goal, and he ended his first full campaign at Stamford Bridge with seven goals and four assists.

Mudryk struggled for Premier League starts in the first months of Maresca's tenure, but was making an impact in the Uefa Conference League when he underwent an out-of-competition test on international duty with Ukraine in October 2024.

Mudryk was provisionally suspended after returning an "adverse finding" for banned substance meldonium.

He was subsequently given the maximum four-year ban by the FA but appealed against the decision to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas).

However, he became free to return to competition "with immediate effect" on 31 July, 2026, after the FA said anti-doping disciplinary proceedings had been resolved and that Murdyk accepted breaking anti-doping rules, also agreeing to a suspension equal to the time already served.

Mudryk, who has always maintained he had "never knowingly or intentionally" taken a banned substance, said he was "grateful" to be able to return to playing after "the most difficult period" of his career.

He will now restart his career at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, 11 miles north east of where it appeared to be falling apart.

title: Premier League breaks transfer record for second straight summer
description: Premier League clubs break their all-time summer transfer record after spending reaches £3.198bn.
fullText:
Premier League clubs have broken their all-time summer transfer record after spending reached £3.46bn.

English top flight clubs had already pushed well beyond the £3bn barrier when Iliman Ndiaye's move from Everton to Manchester City on deadline day for an initial £60m took the amount spent past the previous mark of £3.14bn from 12 months ago.

Enzo Fernandez's move from Chelsea to Manchester City for a joint-British transfer record fee of £125m was then confirmed shortly after the transfer window closed.

A total of £475m was spent on deadline day itself, up from £391m last year.

The total amount spent during the window considerably dwarfs the £1.13bn spent by clubs just five years ago and underlines the power top English clubs have to attract talent, according to figures provided to BBC Sport by Paul Macdonald, founder of FootballTransfers.com.

Follow live coverage of transfer deadline day

Find all the latest football transfers on our dedicated page

All your sport quizzes in one place

Three of the 10 most expensive signings in the history of football have happened this summer – with all of them being Premier League signings. In fact, this summer window featured four of the top flight's five most expensive ever deals.

Fernandez was the headline move, surpassing the £116m Manchester City spent earlier in the window to sign Nottingham Forest midfielder Elliot Anderson, while Chelsea paid £117m to sign Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.

Meanwhile, Liverpool paid an initial £106m, which could rise to £123m, for Paris St-Germain and France forward Bradley Barcola.

Yan Diomande's move to Real Madrid and Anthony Gordon's switch from Newcastle to Barcelona are the only deals completed so far this summer by clubs outside the Premier League to involve fees in excess of £60m.

Tottenham's acquisition of Sandro Tonali was a club-record fee which could reach £100m, while the north London club have also spent heavily on Mateus Fernandes (£85m) from West Ham and Savio from Manchester City (£75m potentially rising to £85m).

Other transfers around this range include the £85.6m deal that City struck to bring in Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille, Bruno Guimaraes' arrival at Arsenal for £75m from Newcastle, and Manchester United landing Cameroon midfielder Carlos Baleba from Brighton for £70m.

So maybe it is not surprising then that in the compilation of the 20 most expensive transfers completed that only six were not to clubs in the English top flight.

Indeed, newly-promoted Ipswich Town have spent more on new signings than the likes of Barcelona, AC Milan, Juventus and reigning European champions PSG.

Manchester City's late confirmation of the signing of Fernandez took their summer spending to £458m as new boss Enzo Maresca was well backed as he looks to build his own team after replacing Pep Guardiola.

That is a new Premier League record for a single transfer window, passing Liverpool's £415m from last summer. While City did spend big, they also made £304m in player sales.

Chelsea were the next biggest spenders as they paid out a total of £349m, although the Blues also sold £382m worth of players to end up with a net profit of £33m.

Tottenham spent the third-highest amount in the summer window with £302m as they hope to avoid another season of struggle and get back to battling at the top end of the table.

Newly-promoted Ipswich spent big in their bid to avoid an immediate return to the Championship with an overall outlay of £171m, outspending Manchester United, who paid out £148m on new signings.

Meanwhile, Hull - also back in the Premier League this season - had a very busy window with a total of 18 new additions, six of them arriving on deadline day.

Premier League clubs as a whole were willing to dip deep into their pockets this summer, as 11 of the 20 clubs broke their transfer records, six of them on more than one occasion.

Coventry, promoted to the Premier League alongside Ipswich and Hull, have done so four times over.

They signed Aurele Amenda for an initial £15.4m, before that fee was surpassed by £20m for Loum Tchaouna. Goalkeeper Carl Rushworth made his loan move permanent for £22m but Caleb Yirenkyi now holds the club record after he signed for £23.1m.

Aston Villa and Ipswich also broke their respective records more than once, while James Trafford (Leeds), Mamadou Sangare (Brentford), Luka Vuskovic (Brighton) and Liam Delap (Nottingham Forest) were all £40m-plus club-record buys.

This summer, 35% of deals involving a transfer fee have been from one Premier League club to another, which is an increase from last year, when the figure was 30%.

That then increases to 44% in instances where Premier League clubs have bought players from lower down the English football pyramid.

On top of that, the Premier League net spend remains over £1bn for this window - by far the most in Europe - despite many of the biggest sales this summer coming from the English league too. Bundesliga and Ligue 1 clubs have received 

Aside from French-based duo Barcola and Bouaddi, the majority of major signings made by Premier League clubs this month have been from rival clubs in the same division.

They include England team-mates Rogers and Anderson, while Newcastle sold Tonali to Spurs and Guimaraes to Arsenal.

Manchester United snapped up Baleba from Brighton after a 12-month chase to aid their midfield revamp, while Tottenham's recruitment of Fernandes and Savio is in the same category.

But why are English clubs buying each other's players more than ever this summer instead of shopping abroad for the biggest deals?

One reason could be the temptation for players who are proven in the Premier League.

Many of last season's big-money signings - with a good chunk of them coming from the Bundesliga - failed to meet expectations or justify their transfer fee.

There have also been deals this summer involving the same clubs, possibly with accounting in mind, with Chelsea and Villa selling players to each other.

And there is also a feeling that teams abroad increase the transfer fees they are asking for when English teams - with all their TV riches - show interest in their players.

title: Camara's £47.1m move from Monaco to Chelsea collapses
description: Lamine Camara is staying at Monaco after the Senegal midfielder's £47.1m move to Chelsea collapses.
fullText:
Lamine Camara will be staying at Monaco after the Senegal midfielder's £47.1m move to Chelsea collapsed.

The 22-year-old completed a medical in France earlier on Tuesday evening but his switch to Chelsea fell through shortly after the transfer window closed at 23:00 BST.

They had two bids rejected by the Ligue 1 side before Monaco eventually lowered their asking price when Folarin Balogun's move to Everton came into renewed doubt.

Chelsea fully expected the move to go through, and had already sanctioned Enzo Fernandez's joint-British transfer record £125m switch to Manchester City in anticipation of Camara joining.

But Chelsea were left furious when the club say they were informed by Monaco in writing that a deal for Camara would not go ahead.

While Chelsea say no explanation was provided, sources with knowledge of the situation have told BBC Sport that they believe Monaco's stance was influenced by Everton's proposed move for United States international Balogun.

Having previously struggled to agree a deal for Camara, Chelsea made a breakthrough when reports claimed Everton's move for Balogun was in doubt.

Sources in France had stated Monaco needed to make a major sale this summer and preferred to sell Balogun. A source at the Ligue 1 club had previously indicated it would take a "substantial fee" to secure Camara's departure.

Camara featured in Monaco's 2-0 win over Marseille on Sunday evening, while Balogun was left out of the squad.

Yet, when doubts emerged over Balogun's proposed move, Monaco's asking price for Camara appeared to fall, making a move to Chelsea more achievable at £47m.

Once Balogun's transfer appeared to be back on track, Monaco appeared to renege on their decision to sell Camara.

BBC Sport has contacted Monaco for comment.

title: Rybakina makes winning start in race to number one
description: Elena Rybakina says she is "motivated" by the race to become world number one but is simply taking things "day by day" after getting her US Open campaign off to a winning start.
fullText:
Elena Rybakina says she is "motivated" by the race to become world number one but is simply taking things "day by day" after getting her US Open campaign off to a winning start.

Playing for the first time since withdrawing midway through her Cincinnati Masters quarter-final with a heel injury last month, Rybakina showed no signs of discomfort as she eased to a dominant 6-3 6-2 win over 17-year-old wildcard Thea Frodin.

The 27-year-old second seed trails Aryna Sabalenka by just 434 points in the world rankings and will become number one for the first time by reaching the semi-finals in New York – even if Sabalenka defends her title.

Regardless of her performance, Rybakina will also secure the top ranking if none of Sabalenka, Coco Gauff and Jessica Pegula lift the trophy.

"I'm definitely motivated [to become world number one]," said Rybakina, who trailed Sabalenka by more than 3,000 points in the spring before the Belarusian entered a mid-season slump.

"I feel like I had opportunities before and it didn't go my way. It will be an amazing achievement but it's still too far and I need to focus on my day off tomorrow, my recovery, and just keep on going."

Fighting to stay No 1 - Sabalenka's US Open mission

Sabalenka wins to begin bid for US Open 'three-peat'

Rybakina, a two-time Grand Slam winner, arrived at Flushing Meadows with question marks around her fitness after retiring injured against Iga Swiatek in Cincinnati.

Though she looked comfortable on court, her movement went largely untested by Frodin - who acted as Serena Williams' body double in the Oscar-nominated film 'King Richard' - as she blew the world number 585 away on serve and dictated points from the baseline.

"We didn't know if [I was] going to be able to play here or not. I'm pretty happy that I'm playing right now, and we are taking [it] day by day," Rybakina said about her injury.

"I was not playing for the full week [before the tournament], so seven days no tennis and basically not too much gym I could do movement-wise.

"So it's a great result after 10 days from that kind of injury."

After opening the rain-delayed match with a double fault, Rybakina proved relentless on serve, dropping just three points and reeling off three consecutive love holds in the first set.

She didn't face a break point until the sixth game of the second set, saving both.

Equally clinical in Frodin's service games, she converted her first three break points to race into a set and 5-1 lead.

However, the young wildcard, making her WTA Tour main-draw debut after winning the United States Tennis Association (USTA) Girls' 18s National Championship, made Rybakina work to get over the line, saving three match points with aces in her final service game among 11 across the match.

Rybakina served out the win with an ace of her own – her sixth of the match and a tour-leading 363rd of the season.

"She played really well today. She has great shots, great serve, it was no easy," Rybakina said of the largely unknown Frodin.

Serena Williams is set for a rematch with Maya Joint, who beat the American great in three sets on her singles return at Wimbledon in June, in the women's doubles.

Williams, partnering her sister Venus at a Grand Slam for the first time since 2022, has been drawn against Australian Joint and Chan Hao-chingof Taiwan.

The Williams sisters, who were awarded a wildcard to compete in New York, won 14 double titles together between 1999 and 2016, including two US Opens.

They were due to renew their partnership at Wimbledon but Serena picked up a knee injury in her 6-3 6-7 (6-8) 6-3 first-round defeat by Joint.
